analysis.one_liner: Requires big political spenders to name their top funders on campaign ads.
analysis.headline: Backed by 49 senators — every Democrat and independent — the bill got one committee hearing and no vote, and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The DISCLOSE Act would have forced corporations, labor unions, Super PACs, and big tax-exempt 'dark money' groups to report campaign spending over $10,000 within 24 hours, name their largest donors, and put the top funders of an ad on the ad itself. It also tightened a ban on foreign money in elections and made it a crime, punishable by up to five years in prison, to set up a shell company to hide foreign political spending [S2]. It was referred to the Senate Rules Committee, received one hearing, and never came up for a vote [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Voters who want to know who is paying for the political ads they see. Today, wealthy donors and corporations can pour unlimited money into elections through groups that never have to name them; this bill would have ended that anonymity for large spenders [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters, and candidates running against anonymous money

how_it_helps.text: Organizations spending more than $10,000 on campaigns would have to report each spending item to the FEC within 24 hours and identify their major funders, under penalty of perjury [S3].
Ads paid for by these groups would have to show a list of the five biggest funders from the past year, so viewers could see who was really behind the message [S3].

The bill would ban foreign nationals from directing U.S. election spending, extend the foreign-money ban to digital ads and state ballot initiatives, and make it a federal crime — up to five years in prison — to set up an entity to hide foreign election contributions [S2].
The FEC would have to audit every federal election cycle and report to Congress on how much illicit foreign money entered it [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Corporations, wealthy donors, and tax-exempt groups that fund political advertising anonymously would lose the ability to hide their identities. Labor unions are also covered and would face the same reporting and ad-labeling duties [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Anonymous corporate and big-money political spenders

drawbacks.text: Groups covered by the disclosure rules include labor unions as well as corporations, so unions would face the same 24-hour reporting and funder-labeling burdens [S3].

The compliance load is heavy: covered organizations must file detailed reports naming funders over $10,000, list beneficial owners, and certify under penalty of perjury, which is a real cost for small nonprofits and unions as well as large corporations [S3].

Supporters of donor privacy argue that naming funders can expose contributors to harassment; the bill tries to address this with an exception for people facing serious threats, but the underlying privacy objection is a genuine trade-off, not a technicality [S3].

The bill itself anticipates court challenges — it includes expedited judicial-review provisions and a severability clause so that if parts are struck down, the rest survives — an acknowledgment that disclosure rules aimed at election spending face serious First Amendment litigation risk [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — knowing who pays for the ads trying to persuade you — is real and goes to every voter, and the bill includes carve-outs for harassment threats and ordinary business income. The costs fall on the organizations spending the money, including unions and nonprofits, in the form of reporting and ad-labeling work, and on donors whose giving becomes public. Whether the privacy cost is worth the transparency is a fair debate; what is not balanced is that the bill never even got a vote.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Rules Committee held a single hearing on the bill in July 2022, never voted to send it to the full Senate, and the Congress ended in January 2023 with the bill dead [S5].

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 25, 2021 and read twice, then referred to the Committee on Rules and Administration, where it sat [S5].
It had 49 cosponsors — 47 of the Senate's 48 Democrats plus both independents, including Majority Leader Chuck Schumer — but not a single Republican [S4].
The Rules Committee held one hearing on July 19, 2022, which was printed as S.Hrg. 117-331, but the bill was never marked up or reported out [S5].
No Senate floor vote ever occurred before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporations, Super PACs, and donor-anonymous 'dark money' groups kept spending on elections without ever having to reveal who funded them. The status quo they benefit from survived intact.

sides.party_line_note: Every cosponsor was a Democrat or independent — 49 of the 50-member Democratic caucus — while none of the 50 Republicans supported it, and the bill never advanced past one committee hearing [S4].

industries.industry: Corporate election spenders and Super PACs
industries.note: These groups would lose the ability to spend on elections anonymously; every major funder of an ad would have to be named on the ad itself. Their interest in keeping donor identities secret runs directly against voters' interest in knowing who is paying for political persuasion [S2].

These organizations are the main channel for undisclosed political spending; the bill would require them to report spending over $10,000 within 24 hours and disclose funders. Their business model depends on anonymity, which voters cannot exercise against them [S3].

Unions are covered organizations too: they would face the same 24-hour reporting, funder disclosure, and ad-labeling rules. A union's members could see where dues money went politically, and unions would bear compliance costs alongside the corporations they often compete against in elections [S3].

Platforms with 50 million or more U.S. monthly users and broadcasters would need to carry and enforce expanded funder labels on political ads, and foreign-money rules would extend to paid digital ads. This adds compliance work but does not change their core business [S3].
